quickExamples.label: BOGO 50% off

explainerNotes.$comment: Free-form prose paragraphs that sit alongside the formulas block in the explainer section.
explainerNotes.text: Two discounts in sequence don't add up. 50% off then 20% off is not 70% off — it's 60% off (because the 20% comes off the already-reduced price). For coupon stacking and Black Friday markdowns, run each discount one at a time.

assumptions: Discount is applied to the original (pre-tax) price you enter.
Stacked discounts (e.g. 50% off then 20% off) are not 70% off — run them one at a time, since the second discount applies to the already-reduced price.
Both decimal comma (12,5) and decimal point (12.5) are accepted.
methodology.rounding: Final price and savings are calculated from the raw input values and displayed to 2 decimal places. Rounding is applied only when the result is shown.
limitations: Sales tax is not added — use the Sales Tax Calculator for the next step.
Shipping, minimum-order rules, and coupon eligibility are not modelled.
Buy-one-get-one and quantity-based promotions need to be entered as their effective per-item percentage.
Retail prices ending in .99 or .95 may show a one-cent discrepancy from a "round" discount — this is intentional, not a calculation error.
If a coupon and a sale apply together, order matters: the coupon usually applies to the already-discounted price, not the original.

faq.$comment: Single source of truth for both visible FAQ and FAQPage JSON-LD. Build pipeline generates JSON-LD from this array — never write a parallel faqSchema[] field.
faq.question: If something is "50% off" and I have a 20% coupon, what's the final discount?
answerParagraphs: 60%, not 70%. The 20% comes off the already-discounted price. $100 → 50% off → $50 → 20% off → $40. Final price is 40% of original = 60% discount total.

faq.question: How do I find the original price from a sale price?
answerParagraphs: Use the reverse formula: original = final ÷ (1 − discount/100).
Example: if you paid $42 with 30% off, the original was $42 ÷ 0.70 = $60. If you paid $60 with 25% off, original was $60 ÷ 0.75 = $80.

This is the inverse of the standard discount formula and is useful when only the sale price and the % off are visible (for example on a tag), and you want to check that the listed discount matches what's actually being offered.

faq.question: Is "buy one get one free" the same as 50% off?
answerParagraphs: Yes, mathematically — assuming you wanted both items. If you only wanted one, BOGO is 0% off (you're paying full price for the one you wanted). 50% off is straightforwardly cheaper for any quantity.

faq.question: Do these calculations include sales tax?
answerParagraphs: No. Discount is applied to the pre-tax price; tax is then added to the discounted total. Use the Sales Tax Calculator for the next step.
